title: The table, many views
hookLine: Mass, Divine Liturgy, Lord's Supper: Catholics and Orthodox say Christ is truly present; many Protestants say spiritually, or by remembrance

lines: A HOST LIFTED, A BELL RINGS.
A SPOON, TRAYS OF CUPS, A RAIL.
cards: This Sunday, in churches of every kind, the same meal will be shared in very different ways. In a Catholic cathedral, a priest lifts a round white host while a bell rings.

In an Orthodox church, a spoon of bread soaked in wine goes onto a child's tongue. In a Baptist church, trays of tiny cups of grape juice pass down the pews. In a Lutheran church, people kneel at a rail.
Mass, the Divine Liturgy, the Lord's Supper, Holy Communion: Christians name it and understand it in genuinely different ways. But everyone is doing what Jesus did the night before he died.
And one of its names is the everyday Greek way to say thank you.

teach.b: Eucharist, from the Greek eucharistia: thanksgiving. Eu, good. Charis, grace, gift.
In Greece today, efcharistó still means thank you.

teach.h: WHEN HE HAD GIVEN THANKS, HE BRAKE IT.
teach.b: Paul passes on that night in a letter to Corinth, in the King James Bible: "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."
Given thanks: that's the verb, eucharisteō. So what happens at that table? Churches differ, in earnest.
Catholics believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood while still looking like bread and wine; they call this transubstantiation.

Orthodox Christians also say Christ is truly present, and prefer to call it a holy mystery rather than explain how. Lutherans say Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine.
Many Reformed and Presbyterian Christians say Christ is truly present, but spiritually, received by faith.
Many Baptists and others see a memorial, a powerful act of remembering, as Jesus said: do this in remembrance of me. Anglicans hold a range of these views within one church.
How often varies too: daily Mass for some Catholics, weekly for many churches, monthly or quarterly for others.
Under the disagreement sits something every one of these churches would say: this meal begins with gratitude.

teach.h: THIS DO IN REMEMBRANCE OF ME.
teach.b: Before anything else, Jesus gave thanks.

how: Christians share the Eucharist, also called Mass, the Divine Liturgy, the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion, with bread and wine or grape juice; Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate it at least every Sunday, while some Protestant churches share it monthly or quarterly.

o: the offering plate passed around during worship
the shared bread and cup, named for giving thanks
a solemn prayer said for the dead at a funeral

p: in, with and under the bread

s: eu, good, and charis, grace. efcharistó is still how Greeks say thank you.
all Christians understand communion the same way

only the gospels tell of the last supper
Paul tells it too, in his first letter to the Corinthians.

games.q: it's the night before he dies. Jesus takes the bread. what does he do first?
games.why: "when he had given thanks, he brake it." the verb is eucharisteō, and the whole meal came to be named for that thank you.

practice: This isn't communion, just an ordinary bite, eaten slowly: hold a piece of bread or a cracker, or imagine one, and think of the wheat, the field, the baker, the hands it passed through to reach you.
Say thank you in whatever way you say it, then take one small bite and taste it. If you pray, give thanks to God; if you don't, give thanks to everyone who brought it to you.

wordCard.voice: Eucharist. Greek for thanksgiving. The Lord's Supper, named for the thanks Jesus gave before he broke the bread.
